title: Attracting tourists
subtitle: off the beaten track, awe-inspiring, unwind
summary: Use the persuasive language of travel writing and holiday advertisements - boasting, wealth of wildlife, stunning locations and unbeatable prices.

lesson.heading: Escaping the crowds
lesson.text: Travel writing begins by promising the reader a way out of mass tourism. To **escape the crowds** is to go where there are not many people; to **get off the beaten track** is to go to places tourists do not normally go; and to **get back to nature** is to live a natural, rural style of life. **Hordes** of people is a deliberately negative word for crowds.

examples.text: If you're the type of traveller who wants to **escape the crowds** and **get off the beaten track**, take a closer look at Suriname.
You won't find **hordes** of people in Suriname.
People who spend all their time in big cities often like to **get back to nature** when they go away.

lesson.heading: The formal language of destination writing
lesson.text: The tourist **sector** is the formal name for the tourist industry. A country may **boast** something - a formal way of listing a place's good qualities. A **discerning** traveller shows good judgement, especially about style and quality, and is often **seeking something out of the ordinary**.

examples.text: Malaysia **boasts** some of the loveliest beaches in Asia.
The tourism **sector** is very important to the economies of many developing countries.
The emphasis is on what makes the country different for the **discerning** traveller.
If you're **seeking** something out of the **ordinary**, why not try a snowboarding holiday?

lesson.heading: Talking about the natural world
rows: plants and animals - a fixed Latin phrase
an area protected by the government for its natural beauty or special history
an area protected to keep safe the animals and plants living there
large areas of land (collocates with large, vast, huge)
original and natural forest, untouched by people

lesson.heading: Rest and energy in advertisements
lesson.text: Adverts promise you two things above all: rest and energy. To **unwind** is to relax and reduce your general level of stress; to **recharge your batteries** is to get your energy back, exactly as you recharge a battery. To **savour** something is to enjoy or taste it, a word used constantly in advertising.

examples.text: **Unwind** in Ubeda, **recharge** in Positano, all from under 800 pounds.
I just want somewhere quiet and relaxing to **unwind** for a week.

examples.note: the heartland = the inland areas furthest from the sea or from borders

lesson.heading: Adjectives that sell a place
rows: filling you with a sense of the power and beauty of what you see
having views of the attractive, natural things in the countryside
no other company can offer cheaper prices for the same service
no other holiday programme can match this
on the edge of the sea or of a river
a perfect place or situation, hot and sunny
organising holidays so that local people benefit and the environment is not damaged

left.label: Gentler
left.text: A **ramble** is a long, pleasant walk, not too demanding. A **hike** is more demanding and suggests more difficult terrain.
examples: We went for a **ramble** along the river on Sunday afternoon.
It's a five-hour **hike** to the top and back.

right.label: Tougher
right.text: A **trek** is usually of several days over wild country. Travel there is often in **4x4** vehicles - said 'four by four', with driving power on all four wheels - across **the bush**, wild areas covered in grass, bushes or trees, especially in Africa and Australia.
examples: A two-week **trek** through the mountains of Nepal.
Taste of **the bush** - ecotourism at its best.

lesson.text: Boast in travel writing is entirely positive: a country boasts fine beaches, the way a brochure lists what it has.

exercises.prompt: Malaysia ___ some of the loveliest beaches in Asia.
exercises.hint: (a formal way of listing good qualities)
exercises.explanation: In travel writing, to boast something is to have it as a fine quality.

exercises.prompt: The tourism ___ is very important to the economies of many developing countries.
exercises.explanation: The tourist sector is the formal name for the tourist industry.

exercises.prompt: It is vital that tourism should not damage the flora and ___ of these beautiful areas.
exercises.hint: (the other half of a Latin phrase)
exercises.explanation: Flora and fauna is a fixed phrase meaning plants and animals.

exercises.prompt: Most tourists like to feel free to get off the ___ track.
exercises.explanation: To get off the beaten track is to go to places tourists do not normally visit.

exercises.prompt: Most people don't like to travel to places where there will be ___ of other tourists.
exercises.explanation: Hordes means crowds, and always carries a negative sense.

exercises.prompt: When I travel, I always try to ___ the crowds and find somewhere quiet.
exercises.explanation: To escape the crowds is to go where there are not many people.

exercises.prompt: There are vast ___ of unspoilt land in the north of the country.
exercises.explanation: Tracts of land are areas of land; the word collocates with large, vast and huge.

exercises.prompt: The country has fabulous national parks and nature ___ where you can camp.
exercises.explanation: A nature reserve is an area protected to keep safe the animals and plants living there.

exercises.prompt: This company is excellent and their prices are ___.
exercises.explanation: Unrivalled means that nothing else can match it.

exercises.prompt: The mountains were so ___. Some were over 5,000 metres high.
exercises.explanation: Awe-inspiring means it fills you with a sense of the power and beauty of what you are looking at.

exercises.prompt: Everyone needs to ___ their batteries now and again.
exercises.explanation: To recharge your batteries is to get your energy back.

exercises.prompt: Order these words from the most physically demanding to the least demanding.
exercises.explanation: A trek lasts several days over wild country, a hike is demanding but shorter, a ramble is a long, pleasant walk.

exercises.prompt: How do you say 4x4, and what does it mean?
options: four by four - driving power on all four wheels
four times four - a vehicle with four seats and four doors
four to four - a vehicle hired for four days
four of four - a convoy of four vehicles
exercises.explanation: A 4x4, said four by four, has driving power on all four wheels, useful on rough terrain.

exercises.statement: If somewhere is described as a paradise in a brochure, that is a negative description.
exercises.explanation: It is strongly positive - a paradise is a perfect place, often collocated with tropical.

exercises.prompt: Match each advertising word with its meaning.

pairs.right: no one offers cheaper prices for the same service
on the edge of the sea or a river
showing good judgement about style and quality

exercises.prompt: Is each expression about the natural world, or a selling word from an advert?
Put this line from a travel article in order.
exercises.answer: What you will find is a wealth of wildlife
exercises.explanation: A wealth of is a formal way of saying a large amount of.
